    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A recent Upcoming York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent Fresh York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    According to recent reports, the city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. Upcoming York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Recent findings suggest that additionally, the new law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani stated.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    • In a recent development, in June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc.
    • In a recent development, but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement.
    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    In a recent development, in June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    In a recent development, but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    Recommended Citation: Nora Collins, Even justices have regrets, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/even-justices-have-regrets/.

    Sources indicate that cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes.     It has been revealed that in an effort to help overburdened federal courts, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators reintroduced a bill Friday that would add 71 latest federal judgeships in phases over several presidential administrations.

    Congress last enacted a significant expansion of the federal courts in 1990, according to a story by Law360.

    The federal courts right now have 677 district judgeships and 179 appellate judgeships. Under the bill, judgeships would be added in a number of states, including Arizona, California, Iowa, Newly introduced Jersey and New York.

    The U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed a version of the bill in 2024, but then-President Joe Biden vetoed it during his last few weeks in office.

    #169955. Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2338 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • In a recent development, every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    In a recent development, every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    According to recent reports, but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    Industry observers note that thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    According to recent reports, three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    It has been revealed that one example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Recent findings suggest that why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Sources indicate that criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    In addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it indicates,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    According to recent reports, for example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    In a recent development, just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    Immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    It has been revealed that last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, major and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 23, 2026, 10:36 am CST.

    Then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks during a news briefing Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).

    A former White House press secretary for President Donald Trump—whose tenure lasted five days in October—is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California after describing herself as a lawyer without being licensed to practice law.

    Katie Zacharia, who graduated with a JD from the Pepperdine University Rick J. Caruso School of Law in 2011, never passed the bar but has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer. A California code says a candidate must have passed the bar exam to be called a lawyer.

    Zacharia has said she worked as the outside counsel to the World Bank, an international financial institution, and as the general counsel for a conservative California nonprofit, according the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit government watchdog group.

    The Campaign for Accountability received a notice of the probe in a Thursday letter from the state bar and told the nonprofit that its complaint was assigned to an investigator and legal adviser.

    “Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” mentioned Michelle Kuppersmith, the executive director of the Campaign for Accountability, in a statement Thursday.

    Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary.

    New White House press secretary calls confusion over legal credentials misunderstanding.

    Industry observers note that is she or isn’t she? Trump’s upcoming press secretary claims she took the bar—in China.

    The marbled murrelet nests in mossy cups on the tall branches of old-growth trees.

    PORTLAND, Ore. (CN) â On the coast of Oregon, the marbled murrelet has long been seen diving into marine waters to forage for fish. But its population has declined, and a conservation group is targeting the Trump administration for allowing its forest habitat to be disrupted.

    The Center for Biological Diversity sued the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management on Monday, accusing the agencies of failing to protect the birds from logging in western Oregon.

    âThe Bureau of Land Managementâs logging practices are undermining marbled murreletsâ already slim chance of recovery in Oregon,â Lia Comerford, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, remarked in a statement.

    The Bureau of Land Management adopted upcoming prepares for almost 2.5 million acres in western Oregon in 2016. The plans were designed to increase logging and maintain protections for murrelets and other species that depend on mature and old-growth forests.

    In a recent development, as part of those plans, the agency consulted with the Fish and Wildlife Service to prepare a 200-page biological assessment on the plans’ effect on marbled murrelets and their habitat. The service concluded the Bureau of Land Managementâs plans were consistent with the Murrelet Recovery Blueprint.

    But two years later, the bureau modified its interpretation of those protections. The group claims the bureauâs new interpretation differs significantly from the version the service consulted on and fundamentally undermines the serviceâs analysis of how the intends will affect murrelets and their habitat.

    According to recent reports, specifically, the group notes the interpretations made it so key protections are triggered far less frequently. The Fish and Wildlife Service then approved those reduced protections, in what the group called a âhighly cursory, incomplete, and arbitrary and capricious manner,â paving the way for logging in murrelet habitat.

    Neither agency made the changes publicly available, the group claims.

    âUnder the first Trump administration, officials at the agency went back on a promise to protect these precious seabirdsâ habitat,â Comerford said. âWeâre not going to let them get away with it.â.

    The marbled murrelet has been listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1992.

    According to recent reports, the seabirds nest high in large trees in old-growth forests and fly up to 55 miles inland during breeding season from late spring to fall. Murrelets nest in small, mossy cups on large branches high off the ground, typically only in large, old trees.

    Murrelets generally lay only one egg per year, leading to the species’ naturally low reproductive rate. Mated murrelets take shifts flying from the nest to the ocean to forage for fish while incubating the single egg. Marbled murrelets have high âsite fidelity,â meaning they often return to the same trees year to year.

    Logging can displace breeding murrelets and lower nest success by removing trees with nesting platforms. Forest clearing can also increase predation. Crows, jays and ravens prey upon marbled murrelet nests and proliferate near forest edges.

    According to the group, scientists have recommended a 300- to 600-foot buffer around occupied murrelet habitat for decades.

    The Major Weekly Elk Project, which the bureau approved in 2021, includes logging in and around nesting habitat. The Center for Biological Diversity claims the bureau is ignoring murrelet protections and has already sold numerous timber sales under the project.

    The group is asking a federal judge to find both agencies violated the Endangered Species Act and block the Bureau of Land Management from authorizing or implementing any logging activities.

    âThe Bureau of Land Management has abandoned the protections it agreed to 10 years ago and is trying to maximize logging at the expense of these very imperiled birds,â stated Comerford. âSadly, the Fish and Wildlife Service is just sitting on its hands, letting marbled murrelets spiral further toward extinction.â.

    The groupâs lawsuit follows the Trump administrationâs announcement of its intent to upgrade resource management prepares for western Oregon to increase logging.

    The Bureau of Land Management declined to comment on pending litigation, but stated it will continue to work closely with its partners to fulfill its public land and conservation responsibilities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

    The full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum showed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

    The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”.

    According to recent reports, in its statement, the law firm states it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”.

    Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under new ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.

    The 11th Circuit panel found that the former Georgia Tech professor's racketeering charges stemmed from an independent investigation by state authorities, not a university audit.

    (CN) â An 11th Circuit panel rejected a former Georgia Tech professorâs suit against two university auditors he blamed for his arrest in a racketeering case.

    Chief U.S. Circuit Judge William Pryor wrote in a unanimous opinion issued Monday that Joy Laskar failed to establish that the auditors, Phillip Hurd and Patrick Jenkins, conducted the investigation that led to his prosecution. Laskarâs charges stemmed from an independent investigation conducted by state authorities â not the university officials’ internal audit or their report of suspected misconduct, the panel found.

    Recent findings suggest that âBefore obtaining an arrest warrant, Agent Vorrasi and McLaughlin conducted an independent investigation,â the George W. Bush appointee wrote in the opinion. âThey reviewed the same documents reviewed during the audit. They spent four months analyzing thousands of documents, deposing Sayana employees and consulting other university officials.â.

    Recent findings suggest that laskar was director of the Georgia Electronic Design Center, a research center where tech companies collaborate with researchers after paying membership dues. He was also co-founder and president of Sayana, a firm that designed and developed high-frequency microchips.

    In a recent development, in 2009, Georgia Tech began investigating a $600,000 shortfall at the center, according to court filings. Hurd and Jenkins learned during their audit that Sayana had billed the design center more than $1 million for the manufacture of prototype microchips which were later sent to a South Korean institute, which paid for the prototypes and research.

    Laskar failed to disclose in conflict-of-interest reports filed with the university between 2007 and 2010 that he had a 42.5% stake in Sayana, according to the auditors. Sayana also did not pay membership fees to use the centerâs resources.

    The auditors reported the suspected malfeasance to the university, which in turn sent the report to the Georgia Department of Law.

    Laskar was charged in 2010 with two counts of racketeering, but a Superior Court judge dismissed the case four years later after finding the statute of limitations barred the charges.

    Laskar filed a civil rights action against the auditors in 2018 in the Northern District of Georgia, claiming the government employees intentionally provided false and misleading information to law enforcement.

    Recent findings suggest that U.S. District Judge William M. Ray, a Donald Trump appointee, initially dismissed the case because Laskar did not receive a âfavorable terminationâ in criminal court, or a finding of innocence, which could maintain a malicious prosecution suit. The decision was reversed on appeal, but Ray dismissed it again last year after finding Laskar failed to support his claims that the auditors operated as law enforcement officers.

    The 11th Circuit panel appeared skeptical of Laskarâs arguments during a hearing this month.

    Recent findings suggest that U.S. Circuit Judge Embry Kidd, a Joe Biden appointee, suggested the auditorsâ recommendation was no different from any other tip to law enforcement.

    âSometimes investigations rely heavily on information provided by others,â he said. âThat does not mean that the decision by the investigator wasnât independent of the people providing the information.â.

    It has been revealed that pryor remarked it did not matter if the auditors provided advice and information to state authorities. The investigators specifically stated that their warrant application was based on their independent investigation and their own assessment of the evidence.

    Recent findings suggest that pryor filed a separate concurring opinion Monday addressing the U.S. Supreme Courtâs decision in Thompson v. Clark, which determined a plaintiff only needs to show that a prosecution ended without a conviction to establish the “favorable termination” element for a malicious prosecution case.

    Pryor defended the use of the common-law tort of malicious prosecution as the appropriate analogy for constitutional claims involving seizures pursuant to legal process, such as arrests based on warrants.

    He distinguished those claims from challenges to warrantless arrests, explaining that the two types of seizures involve different legal considerations.

    U.S. Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa, a Trump appointee, rounded out the panel.

    President Donald Trump imposed the sanctions on judges after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

    MANHATTAN (CN) âÂ A federal judge in Fresh York on Monday noted he doesn’t have the power to stop President Donald Trump from imposing sanctions on judges of the International Criminal Court in the form of frozen bank accounts, canceled credit cards and blocked travel.

    In a recent development, trump declared a national emergency in a 2025 executive order with respect to any ICC effort to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute “any United States person” unless the U.S. formally consents or becomes a state party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC in 2002 to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.

    Judges Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Reine Alapini-Gansou of the ICC turned to the U.S. courts asking to be removed from the sanctions list, unblock their frozen property and bar Trump from enforcing measures against them. But U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman dismissed all but one of their claims and denied a preliminary injunction, finding “deference here is owed not only to the president but also to Congress.”.

    “In short, whatever the courtâs own assessment of the circumstances may be, plaintiffsâ allegations do not permit the court to hold that the president acted ultra vires when he declared a national emergency to address what he determined to be an ‘unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States,’ to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States,” Furman wrote in a 37-page order.

    Each judge was sanctioned over a different decision. Prost, of Canada, and Bossa, of the Republic of Uganda, joined a 2020 appeals ruling that allowed the ICC prosecutor to investigate suspected war crimes and crimes against humanity in Afghanistan. Alapini-Gansou, of the Republic of Benin, sat on the panel that approved arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

    Recent findings suggest that the trio of judges sued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, U.S. Constitution and Administrative Procedure Act. Furman, a Barack Obama appointee, dismissed the due process and takings clause claims, but preserved the plaintiffs’ APA claim accusing the federal government of arbitrary and capricious sanctions designations. That count is premature, the judge stated, since it must be decided on the full administrative record that was before Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he made the decision.

    Furman noted there are three other cases in Manhattan federal court involving challenges to Trump’s executive order, but unlike the others, the trio of judges don’t bring First Amendment claims and are challenging the order in its entirety.

    Industry observers note that those other, earlier lawsuits filed by U.S. human rights advocates resulted in rulings barring the administration from enforcing the order against Americans providing speech-based services to the ICC.

    Trump signed Executive Order 14203 on Feb. 6, 2025, after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

    It has been revealed that after first sanctioning ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, the White House expanded its list to include the international courtâs two deputy prosecutors, eight judges, U.N. Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and three Palestinian human rights organizations: Al-Haq, Al Mezan Center for Human Rights and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.

    The sanctions formally freeze U.S.-based assets and bar Americans from providing funds or services. The judges say their effects ripple across global banks, payment systems and technology companies that rely heavily on the U.S. financial system.

    âThe sanctions regime punishes Judges Prost, Bossa and Alapini-Gansou for having done nothing more than â when called upon to adjudicate matters before them â faithfully discharge their judicial offices by rendering decisions with which the administration disagrees,â the judges say in their lawsuit.

    In addition to arguing that the sanctions strike at the independence of international courts by punishing judges for carrying out their duties, the judges say Trump’s order disrupts ICC investigations that Republican and Democratic administrations alike have backed over the years, including cases involving Sudan, Libya, Uganda, Mali, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ukraine.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Quebec politicians will have to pledge an oath to King Charles III or risk legal battles over their laws.

    MONTREAL (CN) â The Superior Court of Quebec ruled Monday that a 2022 law allowing members of the province’s National Assembly to pledge allegiance only to Quebecers, and not to the British king, is unconstitutional.

    The decision sparked waves of protests from Quebec politicians, putting the upcoming legislative session in limbo.

    Superior Court Justice Ian Demers found the provincial government overstepped its powers by abolishing the king’s oath without the approval of Ottawa and the other provinces. He ruled in favor of Lawrence David, a University of Ottawa law professor who challenged the legislation in August.

    Recent findings suggest that the judge agreed with David that suspending the law is necessary to avoid chaos in the National Assembly. The professor and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute argued that laws adopted by members of the National Assembly who had not pledged their allegiance to King Charles III would be invalid and that the law violated Quebecers’ right to proper representation.

    According to recent reports, david also claimed the oath could be abolished only with the unanimous consent of the provinces and the federal Parliament, because the change encroached on the role of the lieutenant governor. Canada is a constitutional monarchy, and lieutenant governors represent the Crown.

    The Legislature adopted Bill 4 in December 2022, after the three Parti QuÃ©bÃ©cois members elected that year refused to swear the oath required by the Constitution Act of 1867, and were barred from taking their seats in the National Assembly.

    It has been revealed that quebec politicians appear to agree with the law. None of the 127 members of the National Assembly elected in October has sworn allegiance to the king. The court nonetheless found the law unconstitutional.

    “The Constitution is not an Ã  la carte menu in which a subject complies with what suits them,” Demers wrote in his ruling. “Any other proposal would lead to constitutional disorder, or even chaos.”.

    “If the stay were not ordered, all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be reenacted,” he added, predicting the process would only “paralyze” the government and harm Quebecers.

    Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Parti Quebecois leader â and former lawyer â denounced the decision.

    “The government of Quebec strongly condemns a ruling that clearly goes against the democratic will of Quebecers, who have expressed their desire to put an end to the disloyal act of swearing an oath to the British monarch and to the straitjacket of the monarchy in general,” the premier remarked in a statement released on social media in French.

    In a press conference in Montreal on Monday, St-Pierre Plamondon called the ruling a “disgrace” and said he “cannot take an oath to the king of England.” He vowed to take all necessary measures to oppose the judgment.

    Recent findings suggest that the premier noted Quebec never signed the 1982 Canadian Constitution, and that the Constitutional Act of 1867 was imposed on the French-Canadian people after the British conquest of the French territory. He insists Quebecers should be allowed to follow the democratic process rather than be forced to follow rules imposed on them.

    According to recent reports, the legislative assembly set for Dec. 1 is now up in the air. Lawmakers must decide between swearing allegiance to the king and risking court challenges to every decision they make.

    All the opposition parties also criticized the ruling and welcomed the government’s appeal, deploring that the decision could push back further the start of the National Assembly.

    Industry observers note that the Parti Quebecois has long been fighting the presence of the monarchy in Quebec. St-Pierre Plamondon promised earlier this year to abolish the Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, or at least divert its resources to fight complications such as the homelessness crisis.

    Courthouse News reporter Tatiana Mulowayi-Pelletier is based in Montreal, Canada.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Sources indicate that “People think of these kinds of killers as being monsters, but they don’t always present themselves that way,” Conti claims.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 23, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    Sources indicate that it was 1993, and serial killer John Wayne Gacy was on death row. He wanted to hire a First Amendment lawyer to help him fight to keep the profits from the artwork he’d been making while in Illinois’ Menard Correctional Center.

    Recent findings suggest that chicago-based lawyer Karen Conti and Greg Adamski, her husband and law partner, agreed to visit Gacy and talk about representing him. Conti admits she was curious about the man who killed at least 33 men and boys and buried most of them under his house in suburban Chicago.

    Sources indicate that “People think of these kinds of killers as being monsters, but they don’t always present themselves that way,” Conti claims. “He was a bragger and a know-it-all, but he seemed very normal until you thought about what he was saying. He was affable, and he could be charming.”.

    It has been revealed that conti and Adamski, who died in 2011, ended up resolving the First Amendment problems with a “quick negotiation” and then agreed to join Gacy’s death penalty defense team. Conti long had opposed the death penalty.

    Her book on the experience, “Killing Time with John Wayne Gacy: Defending America’s Most Evil Serious Killer on Death Row,” was published in 2024, 30 years after Gacy was executed by lethal injection on May 10, 1994.

    “We were never trying to get him out of prison,” Conti claims. “Our only thought was to have the execution stayed or stopped.”.

    In the book, she describes what it’s like to handle the negative publicity that comes with a high-profile case. In addition, she recounts what she learned from Gacy during her conversations with him.

    “My book is really just about a young lawyer getting involved in something way over your head and how you have to find humanity in something inhumane,” she indicates.

    Because Gacy was a “horrible sexual predator,” some people were angry Conti represented him, thinking she condoned his behavior, she states.

    Gacy was known as being a friendly person who hosted summer parties and dressed as a clown for charity fundraisers and local parties. At the same time, he lured male victims to his house, then raped and murdered them, usually by strangulation or asphyxiation.

    In 1978 he was arrested, and a jury convicted him of 33 murders in 1980.

    During the eight months or so in which she helped file appeals on his behalf, Conti visited Gacy in prison and talked to him almost every day on the phone.

    Gacy, Conti says, had a sense of humor and was “very engaging.” He asked a lot of personal questions and later would draw upon them to manipulate the other person.

    “He wanted to make you feel intimidated or guilty to get what he wanted,” she adds.

    Sources indicate that during one visit, Conti noticed that Gacy had a scrapbook about the victims that he’d compiled. He explained to Conti that he’d wanted to know who “the young men were” who were under his house.

    Gacy treated Conti differently than his other lawyers, she claims, because she was the only woman on his team.

    Industry observers note that “He really liked women,” Conti indicates. “He was oppositional with men, but with me, he was softer.”.

    Recent findings suggest that because he was more cooperative with Conti she was tasked with the “hard communications,” including telling him that the U.S. Supreme Court had denied his last-ditch appeal.

    Industry observers note that “He didn’t seem that upset,” she says. “I think John Gacy was in denial his whole life about who he was and what he did. He was able to compartmentalize. That helped him deny what he knew was coming.”.

    It has been revealed that when asked why it took so long for her to write the book, Conti states that for years “she was very tired of the whole thing,” as representing Gacy had drained her of energy and money. But, she says, she always knew she had a story to tell.

    During the Covid pandemic, she had a little more time on her hands, and she started writing about Gacy.

    “It came pretty easily to me,” Conti says. By waiting to write the book, “I could look at the experience in hindsight.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A woman arrested two years ago for panhandling in a northwestern New Mexico city wants a federal court to find a panhandling ordinance unconstitutional.

    ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. â Rebecca Serrano-Himmel claims she was sitting in a strip mall parking lot with a sign requesting money in March 2024 when police cited and trespassed her from the property. Four months later, she was arrested when displaying a similar sign at an intersection.

    Two years after her arrest, she’s suing the northwestern New Mexico city of Farmington over its sweeping panhandling ban, arguing that holding a cardboard sign requesting money is constitutionally protected speech.

    It has been revealed that in her suit filed Monday in Upcoming Mexico federal court, Serrano-Himmel seeks damages against the city and its police officers for unreasonable seizure and deprivation of free speech, as well as a declaration that the ordinance violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.

    Farmington Mayor Nate Duckett, a defendant in the suit, signed the panhandling ordinance in February 2023. It prohibits the solicitation of money or goods on public and private property.

    “Since the passing of the ordinance and still after the receipt of the letter alerting the mayor and the city attorney about the unconstitutionality of the ordinance, Duckett continued to enforce the panhandling ordinance in a manner that deprived multiple people of their first amendment right to free speech,” Serrano-Himmel writes in the complaint.

    It has been revealed that according to Serrano-Himmel, holding a sign requesting money in a public space is protected speech under the U.S. Constitution and the state constitution.

    This ordinance allowed city police officers to cease her speech and retaliate against her as a result of her exercising her free speech, she says.

    In her first run-in with city police in March 2024, Serrano-Himmel says Officer Aaron Favaloro seized her identification to check for outstanding warrants and issued a citation for panhandling and a trespass notice, despite having no ownership or control over the property.

    Industry observers note that serrano-Himmel asserted throughout the interaction that she was engaging in lawful behavior. In response, Favaloro threatened to arrest her. She was found not guilty of panhandling in July 2024.

    Two weeks later, city police officer Marcus Martinez approached Serrano-Himmel after spotting her walking in a parking lot with a sign stating she was homeless and requesting assistance.

    It has been revealed that serrano-Himmel says Martinez told her she was panhandling, which was not allowed in city limits. She continued to state that she was acting lawfully. Martinez then arrested her for panhandling and criminal trespass and seized her sign.

    Sources indicate that the officers’ actions violate Serrano-Himmel’s First Amendment right, which protects her speech, and Fourth Amendment right, which protects her against unreasonable seizures, Serrano-Himmel writes in the complaint. Both officers are named as defendants in the suit, alongside Duckett and the city of Farmington.

    Serrano-Himmel’s attorney, Joseph P. Kennedy of The Kennedy Law Firm, has challenged the ordinance before, according to Serrano-Himmel.

    Kennedy gave notice to Farmington that non-party Jerry Sullivan was suing the city in August 2023 after Sullivan had been detained for panhandling.

    Sherald Daniels, also represented by Kennedy, sued over the ordinance in another federal lawsuit earlier this year after receiving a citation for playing music in a public space.

    “The city has enforced the ordinance repeatedly in a manner that has damaged and deprived the free-speech rights of residents and visitors,” Serrano-Himmel writes.

    In a recent development, farmington city attorneys declined to provide comment. Kennedy did not respond to a request for comment before publication.

    According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drumsâ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.

    The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their court filings that other alternatives were not fully considered.

    Officials contend that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop in the coming days.

    Lead azide is âvery sensitiveâ and also susceptible to heat, freezing, shock, friction and âall sorts of things that could cause an accidental detonation,â said John Goodpaster, a chemistry professor at Indiana University, Indianapolis. Itâs also old, which increases the risk because explosives become increasingly unstable as they age, he said.

    Add in the environmental threat caused by the lead that will escape into the atmosphere and the challenge is significant, Goodpaster said.

    According to recent reports, âI do not envy the Army,â Goodpaster said. âThey are in a situation where theyâve got a large amount of very dangerous material and not very many good options in terms of trying to dispose of it.â.

    But itâs impossible to predict when it could explode on its own, he said.

    âThe longer we wait, the longer the risk accumulates that they might have an accidental explosion,â Goodpaster mentioned.

    By SUSAN MONTOYA BRYAN and LAURA BARGFELD.

    The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio.
    • Sources indicate that the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • It has been revealed that before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    Sources indicate that the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    It has been revealed that before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    According to recent reports, the previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    In a recent development, early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    In a recent development, at oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    It has been revealed that one striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    In a recent development, justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    Recent findings suggest that the court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    Justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    It has been revealed that brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and mentioned he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    In a recent development, brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Sources indicate that finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    It has been revealed that brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    In closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    Sources indicate that at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC revealed that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    In 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    Industry observers note that the case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws shows the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (269 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Sources indicate that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Sources indicate that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.
