    #169915. The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1819 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • According to recent reports, on November 10, The Newly introduced York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    According to recent reports, on November 10, The Newly introduced York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    According to recent reports, the Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and important source.

    According to recent reports, both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “said in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    Recent findings suggest that in fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Returning to Heller and the phrase at issue, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    In a recent development, so how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    According to recent reports, from there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s Upcoming York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at matter is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    This test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    This is particularly relevant since the court is currently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    Recommended Citation: Andrew Willinger, The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 23, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-second-amendment-and-an-unusually-dangerous-approach-to-dicta/.

    Set priorities and allocate resources across strategic, high-touch partners and scalable paths for emerging and self-serve partners.

    Ensure the team works effectively with Product and Engineering on integration quality, partner onboarding, discovery, activation, and the developer experience across product surfaces.

    Enable the team to work with Marketing and Sales to launch integrations, enable teams, and drive ongoing adoption—not just announcements.

    Establish clear measures for partner-sourced and influenced pipeline, integration adoption, revenue, consumption, retention, and marketplace performance.

    Work with Finance, Data, and Partner Operations to improve attribution, reporting, forecasting, and partner revenue processes.

    Identify risks early, remove blockers, and communicate decisions and outcomes clearly to leadership.

    Have led and developed partner-facing teams, including managers or senior individual contributors, and can balance strategic direction with hands-on execution.

    Have a track record of building partnerships that produced measurable revenue, product adoption, or customer growth.

    Have negotiated complex commercial agreements and understand partnership economics, including revenue share, referrals, and consumption-based models.

    In a recent development, have worked closely with Product and Engineering to ship and grow technical integrations. You can engage credibly with technical teams, including those at AI labs, even if you aren’t the person writing the code.

    Know how to build relationships with executives while earning the trust of product, engineering, and go-to-market teams.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with.
    • That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.
    • Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy firm Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with. First and foremost: child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

    That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.

    Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy firm Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.

    Videos that either included CSAM or featured websites that sell CSAM ran before or after ads from 21 brands, Digiday reports, including Banco Santander, Samsung, Ralph Lauren and Pringles.

    TikTok has avoided taking direct responsibility in its recent statements, assuring advertisers and agencies in a note that it is “deeply committed” to ensuring that TikTok is a safe platform for teens and that it has a task force addressing the problem.

    “We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation,” a spokesperson tells Digiday (uh, duh), adding that it’s “categorically prohibited” on the platform.

    But, so far, these statements have done little to convince advertisers to return.

    “Until we know what’s happening, it’s better to pause,” Laura Camazón, head of digital and innovation at Mediaplus Equmedia tells Digiday. So far, three of the agency’s clients have paused their TikTok activity.

    In a week of mass technology service outages across America, Chase wants you to know that its regular service has not been disrupted.

    However, one or more of Chase’s third-party tech vendors was the victim of a cyberattack. “We believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the bank wrote in a statement on Thursday.

    Sources indicate that mastercard and Visa were also tagged by a ransomware hacker org that leaked customer data. Credit card numbers were not compromised, but the data included some customer details. A Mastercard spokesperson described the leak as only touching a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” The Wall Street Journal reports.

    In a recent development, the disclosures leave many key questions unanswered. None of the companies has named the vendors involved or specified whose data was exposed and what it included. For example, did the leaked data belong to cardholders who consented to having their data used for marketing and analytics? That would be an interesting wrinkle.

    Chase was a little more specific about next steps, though, at least.

    “Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” it said in its response.

    On Thursday, Anthropic IPO’d at a cool $2 trillion, making it the first of the leading AI companies to go public.

    Its share price opened at $111.50, then dropped to roughly $100 within its first hour on the market.

    Recent findings suggest that the timing is striking. Anthropic’s public launch comes just a week after ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his role at the company, following a leaked affair with a woman rumored to be a Chinese spy.

    Huang’s departure left a gaping hole in AI funding. The industry may miss him for other reasons, too, but the bigger concern is capital.

    In a recent development, “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Shamillah Bankiya, a partner at Dawn Capital, tells TechCrunch. Colette Kress, Huang’s temporary replacement as Nvidia’s CEO, is expected to be “much more conservative,” another investor adds.

    Still, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO goes to show that the AI bubble isn’t at risk of popping quite yet.

    But it certainly “contrasts with an anxious moment for investors,” The New York Times writes, amid growing concerns over AI regulation and public backlash against the technology.

    Industry observers note that influencers claim creators can earn up to $5,000 by clipping Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay videos that hit a million views. In reality, YouTube Shorts typically pays just $30 to $100 per million views. [Benzinga].

    In a recent development, also on the influencer front, Instagram creators are skeptical of the platform’s upcoming affiliate program. [The Verge].

    Industry observers note that clinicians can now send prescriptions to patients via ChatGPT. [Adweek].

    Why JCPenney, Nautica, Brooks Brothers and Aéropostale are betting on loyalty programs to keep shoppers – not AI agents – at the center of their customer relationships. [Next in Media].

    According to recent reports, claritas appoints Prem Jacob as its product and technology chief. [Adweek].

    Q3 In Review: Pay TV Shrinks, Streaming And Sports Step Up

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?
    • We figured you’d be busy, and so we tuned in to Q3 call after Q3 call so you didn’t have to.
    • Before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?

    It’s a lot, we know. Not to worry. We figured you’d be busy, and so we tuned in to Q3 call after Q3 call so you didn’t have to. (You’re welcome.).

    Before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept. 30 – and what these reports reveal about the state of TV and media today.

    Netflix’s Q3 numbers look decent on paper. Revenue rose 12% year over year to $12.9 billion, while advertising revenue alone has spiked over 80% this year. But Netflix wasn’t able to double its ad revenue again this year as planned. To be fair, growing ad revenue rapidly was easier to do back when Netflix first started its ads biz from scratch.

    On the advertising front, Netflix also touted improved programmatic targeting and ad measurement capabilities, including a pixel to measure conversions.

    According to recent reports, comcast’s media division reported $5.4 billion in earnings last quarter, a 13% YOY jump from this time last year. Alongside NBCUniversal, which Comcast plans to spin off as a standalone manufacturer alongside British broadcaster Sky, Comcast’s media division also includes NBCU’s Peacock, Telemundo, Bravo and Universal film and television studios.

    In a recent development, but Comcast had weaker performance across the broadband and theme park sides of the business, which saw a 6.1% revenue decline. (The theme parks live under the Universal brand and will go with NBCU and Sky in the spin-off.).

    Industry observers note that unlike Netflix, Fox boasted of recent boosts in engagement. Its free ad-supported TV platform, Tubi, saw a 23% YOY increase in viewing hours, thanks in part to the platform’s recent focus on creator content.

    Zooming out from Tubi, Fox’s overall revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion last quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue. But, sports and streaming aside, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. Fox News saw major viewership declines throughout the year and into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

    Sources indicate that fox was vague about details regarding its acquisition of Roku but asserted it expects to close the deal soon. A mere few days later, on Nov. 6, Fox revealed it officially completed the acquisition.

    Versant Media, which spun off from Comcast in January, posted a 4% decline in Q3 revenue, a loss it mostly blamed on secular declines in the pay-TV industry.

    Versant also closed its acquisition of Full Swing last quarter, a deal that supports its ambitions to lean on live sports – golf in particular – as a competitive advantage.

    Skydance closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 4, so there were no WBD-specific numbers in its Q3 report. But WBD aside, Skydance reported $7 billion in revenue last quarter, representing 5% YOY growth.

    It has been revealed that streaming was a highlight, with Paramount+ revenue jumping 21% YOY to just over $2.1 billion. Skydance also announced prepares to launch a service combining HBO Max and Paramount+ at the beginning of next year.

    Skydance CEO David Ellison confirmed that Paramount+ and Pluto are officially operating on the same ad tech stack, noting that integrating HBO Max should be a relatively speedy process.

    Disney reported a 16% revenue jump to $25.9 billion in Q4 (its fiscal year ends in September) and a revenue increase of 8% to $102.3 billion for the full year.

    Ad revenue grew 10% to $1.7 billion within Disney’s entertainment segment. For its sports segment, that growth rate was 20%.

    Disney also shared that it’s unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app beginning next month. The firm will add more sports to Disney+ in December and introduce creator content from TikTok into the Disney+ mobile app.

    Sports streamer Fubo, which also ends its fiscal year in September, saw its fourth-quarter revenue inch up to $1.5 billion from $1.48 billion during the same period last year.

    It has been revealed that but Fubo suffered a net loss of $51.8 million in its Q4 – a heavier loss than the $38.8 million it posted in the same quarter last year. Fubo attributed the loss to operational and restructuring costs related to its recent merger with Hulu + Live TV.

    Thanks for reading and happy streaming!

    #169899. Ampersand Is Offloading Its Indie Agency Business To Comcast And Spectrum Following Mass Layoffs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (698 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Ampersand Is Offloading Its Indie Agency Business To Comcast And Spectrum Following Mass Layoffs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bridging the gap between linear TV and streaming is apparently easier noted than done.
    • Ampersand, a TV ad platform that combines linear and streaming data from national and local markets to unify audience targeting and measurement, is significantly paring back its business, AdExchanger has learned.
    • The tech giant, a joint venture established in 2019 by Comcast, Charter and Cox (which Charter now owns), will offload its independent agency business to Comcast Advertising and Charter’s Spectrum Reach in 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bridging the gap between linear TV and streaming is apparently easier noted than done.

    Ampersand, a TV ad platform that combines linear and streaming data from national and local markets to unify audience targeting and measurement, is significantly paring back its business, AdExchanger has learned.

    The tech giant, a joint venture established in 2019 by Comcast, Charter and Cox (which Charter now owns), will offload its independent agency business to Comcast Advertising and Charter’s Spectrum Reach in 2027.

    In October, Ampersand sent a memo to clients announcing the decision effective Jan. 1, an Ampersand spokesperson confirmed.

    Ampersand will continue operating, but with a focus on agency holding companies and political advertising.

    The decision comes on the heels of recent layoffs at Ampersand.

    Industry observers note that ampersand didn’t share more details with AdExchanger about the rationale behind its decision to hand off indie agency ad sales. But the client memo, which AdExchanger viewed, reveals some hints.

    Per the memo: “This new model will give independent agencies more direct access to Comcast Advertising and Spectrum Reach’s differentiated capabilities across premium video, streaming, data and technology, advanced audiences, measurement and attribution.”.

    To be fair, media buyers are increasingly seeking more direct access to TV and streaming inventory as they prioritize cost-cutting and ad performance. Indie agencies, it seems, would rather bypass Ampersand as their go-between and tap Comcast or Spectrum directly instead.

    The memo also suggests that indie agencies may value certain capabilities that are unique to Comcast and Spectrum’s ad tech stacks.

    In a recent development, additionally, Ampersand specializes in local TV advertising. So, perhaps indie agencies are less interested in direct access to local TV inventory these days than, say, political advertisers are.

    Meanwhile, Ampersand has been struggling lately, at least judging by recent rounds of layoffs, which the company did not publicly announce.

    There were several significant layoffs over the past year and change, a source with knowledge of Ampersand’s business told AdExchanger anonymously.

    Glassdoor reviews also indicate a bleak state of affairs, along with rumors of the company’s full shutdown. “There have been mass layoffs over the past two years,” a former Ampersand account executive wrote in October. “Most people expect the company to close in the next 2-3 years.”.

    AdExchanger first reached out to Ampersand after hearing rumors of a full shutdown from a source familiar with the firm, but Ampersand denied these rumors and emphasized that it will continue to operate next year.

    Other Glassdoor reviews, however, are similarly pessimistic about the company’s long-term viability.

    The current leadership is “driving the firm into extinction,” another account executive wrote in October while still employed at Ampersand. “Over the last few years, they have done little to develop or improve products or relationships. Instead, they have focused on reducing staff.”.

    Ampersand confirmed to AdExchanger that the decision to offload its indie agency business to Comcast and Spectrum have impacted roles, but declined to share specifics. Ampersand also acknowledged an unrelated round of layoffs in 2024.

    According to recent reports, the future remains uncertain, but what’s clear is Ampersand’s ambitions to focus on reliable sources of TV ad demand: holdcos and political advertising. (And streaming, of course, because, well, duh.).

    Sources indicate that in January, Ampersand launched a new ad platform called TrueStream Political, aiming to help political advertisers more accurately reach voters across connected TV environments. Part of the platform’s pitch is its ability to reconcile audience and identity across disparate CTV platforms, a persistent challenge for CTV media buyers.

    It makes sense for Ampersand to focus more on political ad buying. Political advertisers spent $12.06 billion leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, according to AdImpact, marking the first time a midterm cycle topped a presidential election in terms of ad spend.

    In a recent development, but although political advertising has seen a recent uptick during non-election years, it still tends to be very seasonal. You can, however, bank on a major influx of political ad dollars coming in roughly every two years.

    Industry observers note that so, sure, streaming and political are hot right now. But will this sharpened focus help Ampersand survive into the future? Well … stay tuned.

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re seeking a Technical Account Manager (TAM) to be the primary technical partner for our Team & customers after the sale, helping them adopt, operate, and get long-term value from Supabase.

    At Supabase, TAMs are the technical owners of their assigned accounts, working closely with our most valuable customers to:.

    Understand each customer’s architecture, use cases, constraints, and goals.

    Validate deployments and guide customers through onboarding and early success.

    Proactively surface risks and optimization opportunities before they become incidents.

    Coordinate internal teams on complex escalations and drive root cause analysis.

    Align Supabase capabilities with the customer’s roadmap.

    In a recent development, successful TAMs are proactive, technically credible, and customer-first. TAM is a relationship, not a response channel: you’ll act as an extension of your customers’ teams and advocate on their behalf within Supabase.

    You’ll be joining our Success team, where you will be expected to lead and innovate around the following areas of responsibility:.

    Technical Ownership & Onboarding.

    Act as the technical owner for your assigned accounts, documenting environments, mapping dependencies, and tracking technical risks.

    Validate architecture and deployment prepares after the sale, guide initial configuration and best practices, and make sure customers understand platform capabilities and limitations.

    Help customers reach early success milestones to shorten time to value and reduce early friction.

    Regularly review customer environments and usage patterns to identify scalability, performance, reliability, security, and compliance risks and opportunities.

    Strategy upgrades and lifecycle events, and run architecture reviews for upcoming initiatives, including capacity and growth planning, feature readiness, and early identification of technical blockers.

    Coordinate across Support and Engineering on complex or high-impact complications. TAMs are not frontline support, but provide the context, prioritization, and follow-through that drive resolution, root cause analysis, and preventative action.

    Serve as the voice of the customer to Engineering and Product, sharing specific, reproducible feedback on recurring pain points and taking part in beta and early access programs.

    Partner with Sales and Customer Success on account health and retention, with technical input on renewals, expansions, and evaluations, and early flags on risks to satisfaction.

    6+ years of relevant work experience in engineering, SRE, technical consulting, or similar, including operating production systems under real constraints.

    According to recent reports, strong technical depth across database internals, scalability, security posture, and infrastructure tradeoffs. You understand a customer’s architecture as well as they do, without escalating every question.

    A proactive mindset: you spot risks and optimization opportunities before the customer does, and you treat your accounts like a personal portfolio.

    Sound escalation judgment: you know when to escalate, when to resolve internally, and how to communicate clearly under pressure without creating noise.

    Very strong communication skills. TAMs explain complex problems to non-technical executives and root causes to senior engineers, often in the same day.

    Awareness of how TAM performance shows up in retention and NRR, including surfacing expansion signals and renewal risks early.

    Experience working in async or globally distributed teams.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    According to recent reports, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    It has been revealed that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    In a recent development, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Snap’s Head of Performance Marketing GTM Rick Lucas and Kitsch CMO Ying Ying Kuang on why relying on last-click attribution hides your best customers, and how Clicks + Deterministic Views (CDV) paint a fuller picture of conversion.

    Consumer behavior is changing, and marketers hunting for incremental growth need to look beyond traditional discovery.

    As audiences turn to DMs and group chats to make purchase decisions, standard last-click platform reports miss authentic peer recommendations.

    In this episode of Inside the Stack, Snap’s Head of Performance Marketing GTM, Rick Lucas, and Kitsch CMO Ying Ying Kuang explain why last-click attribution—while still essential—isn’t the whole story.

    They discuss how Kitsch used a 16% geo-lift holdout test to prove Snap’s incremental value beyond the click, why Clicks + Deterministic Views (CDV) are necessary to capture real demand, and how to get comfortable living in the “messy middle” of continuous testing.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (706 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • Recent findings suggest that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime?
    • It has been revealed that people using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    Recent findings suggest that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    It has been revealed that people using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help users pass the time.

    It has been revealed that appLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    Gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    It has been revealed that now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s new Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    Industry observers note that but, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    Sources indicate that the Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    Bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    Industry observers note that to be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    Recent findings suggest that but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    Industry observers note that but there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-upcoming businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    Sources indicate that apple is developing its own autonomous AI agents. [Bloomberg].

    Will Anthropic eventually launch an ads business? [Digiday].

    The Nasdaq enters its third correction of 2026 amid a painful tech investor slide. [NYT].

    A year in review of agency pitches. [Ad Age].

    #169891. Industry News: The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1059 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
    • No organization has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
    • It has been revealed that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the company selling the media sitting in the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

    No organization has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

    It has been revealed that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the company selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

    According to recent reports, so what changed? TTD latched onto a newly introduced principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the company built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

    Recent findings suggest that as DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

    In a recent development, if The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a upcoming era for the company:.

    1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The firm should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

    It has been revealed that 2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

    Industry observers note that 3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

    In a recent development, from the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data said it would work for the buyer.

    TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the tech giant’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

    The business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

    According to recent reports, in 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

    Redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

    Advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

    Industry observers note that the concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

    Television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

    Industry observers note that advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

    Sources indicate that none of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

    According to recent reports, CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only company in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

    According to recent reports, most turnarounds require a company to find a latest reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

    When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

    #169887. AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (694 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Stravito was launched roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.
    • Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution.
    • At the crux of the company is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Stravito was launched roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.

    Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution. Stravito, which touts itself as a consumer intelligence platform, uses AI to help marketers better understand their customers’ preferences and predict their reactions to ads.

    At the crux of the company is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.

    Indeed, it’s the crux of the company name: Stravito is a portmanteau of the words “strategy” and “vito,” which comes from the Latin word for life, “vita.”.

    In September, it released its AI Persona Builder product, which uses brands’ data to develop AI personas that reflect their audiences.

    It has been revealed that stravito connects to a brand’s first-party data as well as other sources, like surveys and syndicated research, plus Stravito’s data from prior campaigns. From there, it builds out different AI personas for different audiences. The personas can represent smaller, more niche audiences, like people from a specific geo to capture “regional nuances,” mentioned Philogène, or broader audiences, like millennials or Gen Z. Marketers can ask a persona a specific question, like why they prefer one version of an ad over another, “and get instant feedback,” he added.

    Coffee brand Lavazza, for instance, conducted several thousand consumer interviews that it was able to integrate into the personas it built with Stravito. When Lavazza was testing different styles of packaging for its Dolcevita line of coffee, it was able to get feedback on the different variations from a relevant customer persona.

    Recent findings suggest that for this particular launch, Lavazza tested its US audience persona, which was built on data, including roughly 5,000 consumer interviews conducted through Kantar and research by the National Coffee Association. The research “covered consumers’ broader attitudes toward life, not only their attitudes toward coffee,” said Philogène, which helped with aesthetic decisions.

    In a recent development, based on the persona’s responses to the colors and other visual cues, Lavazza ultimately changed the packaging color from black to dark blue, Philogène said. It then validated the decision by testing the fresh designs on Meta and comparing engagement.

    Sources indicate that but rather than just spitting out recommendations and hoping that marketers will trust the personas’ responses at face value, Stravito takes a “glass box” approach to AI, noted Philogène. This means that every suggestion and piece of feedback that the AI generates is accompanied by the specific sources and citations that informed it.

    It has been revealed that when your boss asks why you’re making a certain investment, “you do not want to tell them, you know, because AI told me so,” quipped Philogène. Instead, Stravito backs up its decision with the data sources it’s connected to.

    Sources indicate that but no matter how much research a brand or tech vendor has access to, no AI tool can accurately answer every question that someone may pose. And Stravito is exceedingly aware of that. Before a user even asks a question, said Philogène, the AI persona will note topics that it doesn’t have enough data to answer questions about, such as a brand’s pricing model.

    Industry observers note that an AI tool’s lack of knowledge can be “a feature, not a bug,” noted Philogène. It’s crucial for brands to understand what data they’re lacking and where they should commission extra data, he added.

    Stravito’s AI “won’t be sycophantic” and just tell consumers what they want to hear, mentioned Philogène. (Take that, ChatGPT.) Rather, it first determines whether or not it has enough data to answer a given question, and if it does, it specifies whether the answer is explicitly stated in the original source versus inferred. That way, the user can understand the logic backing up every one of the model’s conclusions.

    Having the necessary sources to back up one’s claims and decisions is a crucial facet of journalism, law and research, Philogène said. Shouldn’t advertising be held to the same standard?

    OpenAI’s Fresh Shopping Strategy; What Advertisers Are Thankful For

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.
    • So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.
    • The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

    So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

    The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.

    The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

    It has been revealed that other changes to the documentation are less important, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”.

    Industry observers note that marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search users. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

    Plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently rolled out “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

    But AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

    Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

    On Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

    All that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

    Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

    It’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for owners.

    Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

    According to recent reports, only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research indicates that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

    Ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”.

    According to recent reports, while the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

    Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

    Industry observers note that would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media].

    In a recent development, don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek].

    It has been revealed that microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age].

    Recent findings suggest that after Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the company has appointed its latest CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch].

    According to recent reports, agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post].

    CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog].

    #169883. Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (520 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.
    • It’s a head-scratcher, says Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.
    • “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he claims.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.

    It’s a head-scratcher, says Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.

    “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he claims.

    In a principal media deal, an agency isn’t just advising a client; it’s selling to them. The agency buys media in bulk with its own money, then resells it to the client – usually without saying what’s in the package or what it paid – and then keeps the difference.

    Which raises an obvious question: Is the agency recommending what’s best for its client or what’s best for the agency?

    To understand how the industry got here, Asghar claims, you have to go back around 25 years to when media buying was unbundled at the behest of procurement and agencies started pooling client dollars to gain leverage. The original idea was to pass along the savings.

    But after the ANA’s K2 report came out in 2016, it became clear that agencies were holding onto big volume rebates for themselves.

    Recent findings suggest that “They’re not actually savings; they’re profit,” Asghar indicates. “And they’re about the purest form of profit a company could attribute to their bottom line.”.

    Recent findings suggest that today, holding companies have repackaged those rebates as principal deals, which is really just arbitrage. Asghar argues that this money should go back to the client.

    In a recent development, not that any of this is happening secretly, though. Defenders of principal media like to say it’s fine as long as clients opt in. But Asghar isn’t buying it.

    It has been revealed that “It’s one thing to know it’s happening,” he indicates. “It’s another thing to know what’s happening inside of what’s happening.”.

    In other words, marketers can sign off on a principal deal and still have no idea what ended up on the initiative. They often can’t get log-level data showing where their ads ran or what they originally cost. And because agencies buy the inventory at undisclosed discounts or through volume rebates before reselling it at a markup, the true price is hidden.

    Marketers should go back to buying media separately from planning and strategy services, Asghar says, so the agencies giving advice aren’t also the ones with inventory to move.

    Otherwise, Asghar states, an agency isn’t really acting as an agent.

    Being a fiduciary, he states, “means you have a responsibility to do what’s in the best interest of [clients], not just what’s in the best interest of you or your shareholders.”.

    In a recent development, also in this episode: Why AI is going to “make dumb companies dumber and smart companies exceptional,” why young planners still need to learn the old-fashioned way even if agents can do some of their work for them and why attribution and measurement are the “dry turkey” of ad tech. (It “looks great on the outside,” Asghar quips, “but it’s terrible on the inside.”).

    Another Disney creator deal: YouTube illusionist Zach King joins the Mouse House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.
    • For their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute.
    • One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A Newly introduced Hope.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.

    For their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute. Disney notes the agreement “will also bring [King’s] signature illusions to latest content for Disney+ and [King’s] own channels inspired by Disney’s Hexed, Star Wars, and other Disney films and experiences.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A Newly introduced Hope. King uploaded the film to YouTube in August, and soon will cross-post it to Disney’s streaming service.

    A post shared by Zach King (@zachking).

    But there’s still more: King will pop up on Disney’s social accounts as well, hosting behind-the-scenes content about the VFX and filmmaking techniques he uses in his content.

    “I fell in love with filmmaking and storytelling as a young kid, grabbing my parents’ home video camera and teaching myself to edit,” King wrote in an Instagram post. “A lot of my early homemade films were inspired by the Disney movies and the behind-the-scenes footage they would show in the DVD featurettes. There was always a sense of magic I would see on the screen, and so I’m thrilled to be working with Disney to continue that magic of filmmaking for the next generation of storytellers.”.

    Recent findings suggest that king has worked with Disney regularly in recent months: He was at its glitzy Created in L.A. event in September, and earlier this month played a game of viral format Cake or Fake? with Hexed (and Arcane, and Sinners, and Spider-Verse, and Hawkeye) star Hailee Steinfeld. But this is his first official, expansive content deal.

    In a recent development, “Zach makes the impossible look real, bringing the kind of imagination and originality that has always defined Disney,” Asad Ayaz, The Walt Disney Tech giant’s CMO and Brand Officer, said in a statement. “He brings both a filmmaker’s ingenuity and a fan’s passion to our stories, along with a unique connection with audiences. We want to build lasting relationships with creators like Zach, giving their ideas room to grow across Disney. That’s what makes this next chapter of our work together so full of possibility.”.

    As we mentioned above, everyone–including YouTube–has had their eye on Netflix’s obvious poaching efforts…leaving room for Disney to sneak in the back.

    In a recent development, in the last couple months, Disney has unveiled deals with major creators Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect, and Like Nastya. Crucially, these are all development deals–the exact kind of agreement that has YouTube on guard with Netflix.

    And Disney’s not quite showing its full hand just yet. During its earnings call Nov. 17, executives only mentioned YouTubers once, in passing and in reference to Disney+’s growing crop of approved creator content.

    We suspect more is in the pipeline–and that YouTube may have to start paying creators to turn down Disney deals, too.

    #169873. Netflix is rallying post-Warner Bros. with revised IRL installation aims and a potential bid for NBCUniversal

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (613 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Netflix is rallying post-Warner Bros. with revised IRL installation aims and a potential bid for NBCUniversal

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros.
    • That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Substantial Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.
    • In a recent development, well, according to Bloomberg, the current initiative is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery.

    What if it bought NBCUniversal, tho?

    That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Substantial Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, well, according to Bloomberg, the current initiative is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses. The streamer first unveiled these in 2023, with a demo setup that looked like someone stocked the gift shop in Jurassic Park with merch of the laser murder doll from Squid Game.

    At the time, Josh Simon, Netflix’s then-VP of Consumer Products (now CEO of collectibles company Funko) said the concept for Netflix Houses came from knowing “fans love to immerse themselves in the world of our movies and TV indicates,” and “thinking a lot about how we take that to the next level.”.

    Netflix had flirted with pop-ups before that; those were mainly focused on selling stuff. Make no mistake, Netflix Houses are also focused on selling stuff, but in a Disney World kind of way, where fans pay $39 to enter the House and head through an art gallery-esque space filled with themed exhibits like exclusive theater shows, movie/TV set recreations, VR experiences, and arcade games. There are cafeterias and merch shops, but by and large the things to buy share billing with things to do.

    The Houses are permanent installations (for now just in Dallas and Philly, with one planned to open in Vegas in 2027) but the exhibits within rotate regularly to keep up with whatever’s trending on Netflix.

    This year, for example, the Houses were renovated to feature animated smash megahit KPop Demon Hunters. They’ve also spotlighted Stranger Things, One Piece, Wednesday, and the aforementioned Squid Game.

    It has been revealed that per Bloomberg, Netflix initially planned to open dozens of Houses across the U.S., focusing on quieter suburban areas away from downtowns. It wanted to snap up spaces in malls, which are not doing very well and might be willing to rent for cheap.

    But apparently the results from its first two Houses haven’t been quite what Neflix expected, so it’s pausing openings beyond Vegas until it can reassess.

    In a recent development, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the Philadelphia location has daytime draws like mini golf and a movie theater, but doesn’t see much traffic at night. Dallas, meanwhile, is breaking even financially, and has done well with larger groups and corporate events.

    Recent findings suggest that netflix is also planning to see what comes from its Las Vegas location. Vegas, as you may know, is not in fact a quieter suburban locale–so if the House there proves to be profitable, with more traffic than Dallas and Philly, Netflix could reconsider where it opens in the future.

    According to recent reports, people familiar with the matter noted Netflix is also looking at maybe taking Houses overseas. But wherever the next one ends up, it probably won’t open for at least another year, they said, until significant data from all three flagship U.S. locations is in.

    Now, with all this in mind, it’s worth remembering Netflix just shock-fired its longtime Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and replaced her with Peter Rice, Disney‘s former General Entertainment Chairman. Film chief Dan Lin is out too. Clearly, Netflix hopes to revamp more than its IRL installations…and perhaps it’s hoping Rice’s Disney EXP comes in handy with the Houses?
